Article Title: When 4x4 becomes weapon of intimidation
Article Text:
A black SUV aggressively swerves across lanes on a busy Delhi highway, cutting off a sedan and two-wheelers. (AI image)

'Has to be an SUV': A string of recent incidents across Delhi-NCR involving aggressive driving prompted TOI to reach out to experts to examine the psyche behind road rage. The common refrain: it's not the car, it's the driver.

..

Gaurav Gill, Arjuna awardee and rally driver says, “They think with these cars, they own the road. But ultimately, it is not the car, it is the person driving it.”

What research says

Bani Yadav, rally driver says, “I can easily beat them at this game, but this is not a game I want to play on the roads. I would rather do it on the track.”

Riya Yadav says, “These vehicles are designed for off roading, the problem is the psyche, and rash driving, not the vehicles.”





NEW DELHI: When Gaurav Gill takes his car out on Delhi roads, it is not unusual for someone to try to race him. Bani Yadav faces much the same on Delhi-Gurgaon Expressway when she is out in her fancy SUVs.Cars pull up alongside them, cruise wheel to wheel, drift slightly into their lane or surge ahead only to slow down — all familiar gestures from motorists trying to catch their attention and challenge them to a race.The irony is hard to miss. The two are among India’s fastest drivers and can put these people far behind within seconds.Gill, an Arjuna awardee, is the first Indian driver to win the overall FIA Asia-Pacific Rally Championship. Bani is the only woman in India to win all major cross-country rally titles in a single calendar year. They have built careers around speed, but when it comes looking for them on NCR roads, neither takes the bait.They call such motorists “delusional” and people with little idea of what triggers an accident. Not because they cannot race, but because they know there’s a place for speed and competition and pushing a car to its limits.It is just not a public road, the two say. “I can easily beat them at this game,” Bani says. “But this is not a game I want to play on the roads. I would rather do it on the track.”The behaviour they describe is increasingly playing out in disturbing forms on Delhi-NCR roads, not just in the form of racing or aggressive overtaking, but in using SUVs to intimidate, chase, hit or deliberately ram other road users.This Sept alone, a series of incidents put SUVs in the spotlight. On Sept 2, two people were killed after a speeding SUV hit their motorcycle in Delhi Cantonment.On Sept 18, following a dispute, an intoxicated driver repeatedly rammed a commercial cab with his SUV in Sector 89, Gurgaon. The impact was violent enough to deploy the cab’s airbags and severely crush its side.On Sept 26, an SUV was captured on dashcam weaving aggressively through traffic near Dwarka Expressway. It attempted to squeeze through a narrow gap, knocked down a motorcycle and injured two riders before speeding away.These and many other incidents in recent times involve reckless driving and deliberate acts of road rage. Their recurrence raises a bigger question: What is it about a section of drivers that turns a large, powerful vehicle into an instrument for asserting dominance on the road?Gill believes the answer begins much before a person gets behind the wheel.“We, the racers, have spent decades trying to get control cars, yet we do not overspeed on roads. There are certain cars, which have a muscular and macho image these people think goes with their personality. And then these elements think that with this car, they own the road. And it starts with the way they inculcate values in their homes. So, it is down to not the car but the person driving it,” he says.Bani says some motorists feel the need to show they are faster, stronger and more powerful than others.“Some SUV drivers think they can get away with breaking the law. I think policing here is not strong enough, or even when action is taken, these people know they will ultimately get away without facing a major punishment. When there is nothing much to deter them, they think they are the law unto themselves. We require stricter laws that deter these people,” she says.Bani, who is India’s fastest woman rally car driver, says, “I can understand that people may get an adrenaline rush from driving fast, but they should channel this positively. They should enter motorsports and showcase their talent on the tracks. If you have a passion for fast driving, that is your choice, but you do not have the right to punish others.”Experts caution against turning SUVs into villains. Gaurav Vangaal, associate director, production forecasting, Mobility Global, says SUVs constitute over 55% of passenger vehicles sold in India and have overtaken sedans and hatchbacks in popularity over the past decade.“So naturally they are far more visible on our roads and in case of such incidents,” he says.Road accidents broadly fall into two categories: those in which a driver unintentionally loses control, is fatigued or misjudges traffic, and those involving reckless behaviour like overspeeding or not stopping after an incident.“Some recent cases have involved SUVs, which has put the spotlight on the vehicles themselves,” he says. “But we need to separate it from its driver’s conduct.”Indian roads are shared by cars, two-wheelers, pedestrians, cyclists and even animals, making the driver’s responsibility critical irrespective of the vehicle being driven.There is, however, a possible psychological element to the way larger vehicles can influence their drivers.Piyush Tewari, founder and CEO of SaveLIFE Foundation, points to emerging evidence suggesting that concerns about risky SUV driving are not merely anecdotal. He cites a 2024 study involving 546 licensed drivers across India and published in ‘Transport Policy’.It found that SUV drivers reported significantly riskier driving behaviour than drivers of sedans and hatchbacks, with speeding emerging as an important predictor of such behaviour.International studies have also described what researchers call the “car cushion effect” — the possibility that the greater size and perceived protection of a larger vehicle can give drivers an increased sense of security and control, which can in turn encourage risk-taking.In one controlled driving-simulator experiment cited by Tewari, participants who believed they were driving a larger vehicle displayed riskier driving than those who believed they were driving smaller ones, even though the underlying simulator settings were the same.That becomes particularly relevant with SUVs because many combine greater size and mass with high engine power, acceleration and a sporty positioning.“These characteristics should demand greater responsibility from the driver, not encourage a more aggressive driving style,” Tewari says.He also cites a study by Insurance Institute for Highway Safety in US, which found that vehicles with particularly tall front ends were around 45% more likely to cause a pedestrian fatality in a crash than vehicles with lower, sloping front ends.But even that, he says, should not become an argument against SUVs. “The answer is not to demonise SUVs or their owners, but to recognise the interaction between vehicle characteristics and human behaviour,” Tewari says.The larger concern, he feels, is enforcement or the lack of it.“Enforcement against speeding, dangerous overtaking and other forms of rash driving needs to be strengthened, while vehicle manufacturers also have a responsibility to ensure that the marketing of power, speed and performance is accompanied by an equally strong emphasis on responsible driving. Ultimately, the greater the capability and potential impact of a vehicle, the greater the responsibility that must come with driving it,” he says.Riya Yadav, the youngest female rider at 19 to conquer Khardung La in Ladakh, says the physical characteristics of an SUV could also play a role in how a driver perceives the road.SUVs have a higher seating position because they are designed to provide greater ground clearance, keeping the main body of the vehicle above rocks, water and deep potholes, she explains.“This tall build gives the driver a commanding, high-up view of the road and the front bonnet so that you drive safer, but inadvertently it does make you feel that you are above all,” she says.But that, Riya stresses, does not mean everyone driving an SUV develops an aggressive mindset. “In Delhi, many women drive these vehicles. But they rarely feature in any of the videos of rash driving and road rage that go viral.”The changing composition of India’s car market has made SUVs a much more visible presence. They account for over 55% of total passenger vehicle sales nationally, vastly outpacing traditional hatchbacks and sedans.With more such vehicles on the road, their proportion of involvement in traffic incidents will naturally increase. But the question is whether their increased visibility is also making certain forms of aggressive driving more visible.Former special commissioner of police Muktesh Chandra believes cops should look beyond the driving offences in identifying patterns.“There are some traits you will find in these vehicles, including casteist stickers and VIP numbers. Once I saw an SUV owner using ‘8055’ on the number plate in a way it read like ‘BOSS’,” he says, adding that police should undertake special drives.For Nand Gopal, former motor licensing officer with Sarai Kale Khan Regional Transport Office, the issue starts even before a driver gets his licence.Gopal, who implemented Delhi’s first automated driving test track in early 2018, believes the licensing system needs to do more than assess whether a person can manoeuvre a vehicle.“The entire learner’s driving licence test has been moved online, and you can even take it from home. Naturally, this increases the risk of people trying to game the system,” he says.Driving tests focus more on road manoeuvring and assessing a person’s driving skills than on teaching them how to drive responsibly and protect other road users, he says.“It is not that these aspects are missing from the govt-prescribed course, but hardly anyone is aware of them,” he says, adding that drivers need to be trained to remain mindful of smaller vehicles and other road users.That becomes particularly important on roads when an SUV, a motorcycle and a pedestrian find themselves sharing the same limited space within seconds.Training, he says, should also cover what a driver should do after an accident.“The manual states that in such an event, one should provide first aid to the victims, if possible, and help them get medical attention. We also need to teach people the human side of this — why such actions are important and how they can help even in case of an FIR as the law takes your intentions into account as well.”
Article Summary: A string of recent incidents across Delhi-NCR involving aggressive driving prompted TOI to examine the psyche behind road rage. The common refrain: it's not the car, it's the driver. This Sept alone, a series of incidents put SUVs in the spotlight. On Sept 2, two people were killed after a speeding SUV hit their motorcycle in Delhi Cantonment.

Article Title: Diwali party season is here. But who is RSVPing?
Article Text: In just a few days, most of our chat inboxes will be filled with card-party invites, Karwa Chauth get-togethers and Diwali parties. Some will be expected, while others will come from people whose parties you have never attended in the past. Almost every invite will mention RSVP details, and some will even carry a polite request -–‘Kindly RSVP’ – both of which will be conveniently ignored and treated as almost as irrelevant as the time mentioned on the invite. After all, who even RSVPs?The original idea behind RSVPing is simple: Help the host plan efficiently by knowing in advance how many people will actually turn up. But somehow, the concept doesn’t quite hold true for most of us. In Delhi, saying yes to an invitation is rarely the final word. It is, at best, a tentative expression of interest. Our decision to attend a party depends on several factors. First, how have we been invited? Was it just a WhatsApp forward, was it followed by a phone call, or did someone make the effort to personally invite us? The decision to attend or not attend can change depending on how important we feel the invitation was.Second, there is the commute and traffic situation on a given day. It is highly unlikely that someone in Noida would readily commit to a party at a Gurgaon farmhouse on a weekday. That RSVP requires not just enthusiasm but also considerable faith in the Delhi-NCR traffic. Third, how much social hopping does one have to do that evening? During the festive season, attending three parties in one night is hardly unusual, which means your arrival at party no 3 depends entirely on how long you stayed at party no 1 and whether you ever managed to leave party no 2. And fourth, perhaps the most important question, will we have appropriate company at the party? Who else is going? Is the friend we planned to go with still going? Can we bring a plus-one? A confident ‘yes’ on Monday can easily become a ‘let’s see’ by Friday evening.There can be many more additions to this list, but the point is that most of us seem to find RSVPing an irrelevant exercise. It is something we may customarily say yes to when we receive an invitation, but that answer remains open to revision until almost the moment we leave home. And sometimes even after that. The reverse is equally true. Someone who never confirmed may suddenly message at 8.30pm asking, “Party still on?” and arrive with another person in tow. For the host trying to calculate food, drinks, seating, staff and parking, the guest list can therefore remain a moving target right until the doorbell starts ringing.Even hosts are now used to the fact that few people will RSVP in advance, even when they personally call to invite guests and request a confirmation. In a casual chat, a Delhi host who plans a Diwali party every year said that in the last six years since she has been hosting parties, it has never happened that guests have confirmed their presence or taken the RSVP seriously. Yet, she says, the turnout has usually been better than expected. “It would be so much easier if one gets the RSVP in advance, especially for Diwali parties, mostly planned at a grand scale and involves a lot of pre-planning. Now that we have been organising these parties from some years, we just go by last years’ guest list, the regular ones and those who always say they will come but never come.”Perhaps that is the real Delhi RSVP system. Hosts no longer count confirmations, they rely on experience, previous guest lists and a mental database of who always turns up, who never does and who will say “on my way” while still deciding what to wear.So this festive season, when an invitation lands in your inbox with ‘Kindly RSVP’ printed neatly at the bottom, spare a thought for the host and actually respond. And if you say yes, try turning up too. Now that would be a festive season surprise.
Article Summary: In Delhi, saying yes to an invitation is rarely the final word. It is, at best, a tentative expression of interest. A confident ‘yes’ on Monday can easily become a ‘let’s see’ by Friday evening.

Article Title: Dr Kotnis international humanity award to V Shantaram
Article Text:
Commemorating the 80th anniversary of Dr Kotnis Ki Amar Kahani, the remarkable director V Shantaram was posthumously honored for shedding light on Dr Dwarakanath Kotnis’s heroism

Dr Kotnis Ki Amar Kahani





MUMBAI: Eighty years after he immortalised the fascinating story of Dr Dwarakanath Kotnis through the 1946 film, legendary filmmaker V Shantaram has received the Dr Kotnis International Humanity Award posthumously."Not many were aware of the life and times of a young doctor Kotnis who died serving the Chinese soldiers during the World War II till V Shantaram made Dr Kotnis Ki Amar Kahani. Recognising his contribution in immortalising Dr Kotnis, we decided to give this award to him posthumously. His son and former Sheriff of Mumbai Kiran Shantaram received this award," said Rajendra Jadhav, chairman of the Dr Kotnis Memorial Committee.Dr Kotnis was part of a team of five doctors who had set sail for China on September 1, 1938, to help the Chinese army during the Second Sino-Japanese War in the 1930s. While the other four physicians returned to India, Dr Kotnis stayed back, fell in love with a Chinese nurse whom he married, but died young because of the inclement weather he faced there. Dr Kotnis is a much-revered figure in China, which considers him a great “friend”.As India and China improve their relationship, the award adds to the enduring "friendship" between the two neighbours.Those who attended the event included Consul General of China in Mumbai Qin Jie, Kiran Shantaram, and Dr Kotnis's nieces Dr Sumangala Borkar and Nirmala Kotnis.
Article Summary: Dr Kotnis Ki Amar Kahani immortalised the story of Dr Dwarakanath Kotnis through the 1946 film. Dr Kotnis was part of a team of five doctors who had set sail for China to help the Chinese army during the Second Sino-Japanese War in the 1930s.

Article Title: The other side of September 30: How a family waited anxiously to see thier injured son Captain Smit Machchhar
Article Text:
For Smit Machchhar’s family, the past few days have been a blur of fear, faith and waiting





MUMBAI: To the world, September 30 was the day a terror attack was thwarted. To Captain Smit Machchhar’s parents, it was the night their only child lay wounded and alone in a military hospital in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia , deep lacerations across his body, tubes running in and out of him.While the world was already beginning to call him a hero, his parents in Mumbai were still living inside the uncertainty of those first terrible hours. They had no clear word on his condition. No assurance that their son would survive. They were trying to find a flight to him, but airline schedules offered little mercy. There was nothing left to do but pray.It was only around 10am on Thursday that they managed to board a flight. Even then, they were flying only as far as Dubai, still hundreds of miles from where their son lay.“I was on the plane in Mumbai when Prime Minister Narendra Modi called; he told me not to worry and asked me what I wanted. He said, ‘Before the day ends, I will make you speak to him’,” Smit’s father, Upendra Machchhar, told TOI in an exclusive interview from Dubai.By the time the family landed in Dubai, another development had already begun to unfold. Indian Embassy had contacted Smit’s wife, Sonal, and informed her that Capt Machchhar had been airlifted on Dubai Sheikh’s private aircraft to be taken to the military hospital in Abu Dhabi.The family set off for Abu Dhabi, a journey of about two hours. There was relief now, but it was not yet peace. They knew he was alive. They did not know how badly he had been hurt.It was only after Upendra finally saw his son in the hospital that some of the fear began to loosen its grip.“After yesterday’s visit to the hospital, I am now at some comfort level and believe that everything is going to be fine. Smit also tells me, ‘Give me some time and I’m going to be all good’,” said the father.For the Machchhar family, the days since the attack have blurred into one long stretch of fear, faith and waiting. Their son has become, almost overnight, an international symbol of courage. But for them, beneath the headlines and the praise, he remains what he has always been: their only child.“The cuts are deep, and he is in terrible pain. But when leaders of nations speak to him, he gathers himself and responds with remarkable calm,” Upendra told TOI. “As his family, we know what lies behind that calm. The stress is immense. But the God who saved him will also decide the course of his life ahead. Right now, we are 100% positive that God will do what is best for him.”The hospital has told the family that recovery will not be quick. “The head of the hospital said he needs at least another eight days. After that, they will review his discharge date. The wounds and cuts are very deep. They want him to be completely fine before they send him home. But the treatment has been fantastic.”Yet for Upendra, there is another question that refuses to leave him. It is not how his son endured the injuries. It is what made him open the cockpit door at all after being stabbed.“What happened shocked us. But it’s his bhaav (his intrinsic nature) to place others before him that made him do what he did,” the father said. “If we have a family event and if he has to go to mentor another pilot or go to conduct a pilot test, he will prioritise that and ask the family to push the function by an hour or so.”Upendra believes that instinct, to put someone else first, was there long before Smit ever became a pilot.Flying was not the family plan.Smit was initially expected to join the family business. His grandfather had established a textile printing factory, and Upendra and his brother eventually took over its running together. Smit studied at SASMIRA, as did his cousin. After completing his course, he pursued management studies and then began spending time at the factory alongside his father.But it was the arithmetic of the business that unsettled him.“He told me, ‘We shell out more every day than what we earn.’ I told him, this is how this business works; it has been like this for generations. But he wanted to change a few things,” Upendra said.Then, one morning, Smit came to his father with an entirely different request. “He asked me for permission for something he wanted to do. He said, ‘I have a dream I want to chase’.” The dream was to fly.“I told him, are you getting carried away? Every penny is hard-earned. I told him that if he promised not to waste the money, I would let him go.”Upendra has one son. His brother had one son too. As it turned out, Smit’s cousin also wanted to become a pilot. The two families sat the boys down and told them what they were committing to. “It was a huge expense. We told them not to waste the money.”They didn’t.Smit went to New Zealand for his training and completed it in 10 months. Then came another call from his mentor: if the family could put in another Rs 26 lakh, Smit could obtain a type-rating on a Boeing 737. He went to London and trained on Boeing aircraft. Soon after, he joined SpiceJet.“It has been 11-12 years now,” his father said.In 2022, Smit received an interview call from flydubai. He got the job and eventually moved to Dubai with Sonal.The couple wanted his parents closer too. For the past four years, Upendra and his wife have divided their lives between Mumbai and Dubai, spending roughly six months in each city.He was due to return to Dubai on Oct 25 anyway.Instead, he found himself flying there much sooner, summoned by the worst phone call of his life.For one night, Sonal was alone with the uncertainty of what had happened to her husband, Upendra said. When she later told his parents what she had gone through, the weight of it became unbearable.“We started crying a lot,” Upendra said.The early hours were the hardest because there was so little certainty. There was no clear picture of what had happened, no way of knowing what the next few hours would bring.And yet, somewhere in those hours, the family made a decision. They would not keep returning to the attack. “We decided not to speak of the incident.”For now, they want to look beyond September 30. Towards the day Smit walks out of the hospital. Towards the day the wounds have healed. Towards the day the pilot who has spent years learning the discipline of the skies can return home.
Article Summary: Captain Smit Machchhar's parents still living in the uncertainty of those first terrible hours. They were trying to find a flight to him, but airline schedules offered little mercy. It was only around 10am on Thursday that they managed to board a flight. The family set off for Abu Dhabi, a journey of about two hours.

Article Title: A self-funded centre keeping Gandhian flame alive in Marathwada
Article Text:
Mahatma Gandhi Sarvodaya Bhavan

Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar





: A building in the Silk Mill Colony of Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar has been quietly keeping the Gandhian thought alive for both younger and older generations.Known as the Mahatma Gandhi Sarvodaya Bhavan, the hub serves as a critical reference point for students, activists, and researchers seeking to explore Gandhian literature, khadi spinning, and the core concept of Sarvodaya—the welfare of all.Dnyanprakash Modani, the 77-year-old Gandhian thinker, who started the full-fledged centre to coincide with the 150th birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi in 2019, said that the principles and methods of Gandhiji can still strongly appeal to modern audiences if they are presented through a contemporary lens.“With its inclusive approach, our centre brings together Gandhians under one roof, making it one of the few surviving spaces for non-violent, secular, and democratic discourse in the region,” he said.A full-panel pictorial exhibition titled ‘Mohan se Mahatma’, tracing the journey of Mohandas to the Mahatma, is one of the highlights of the centre.“The evolution of Gandhiji from a commoner into a towering personality revered as the ‘Mahatma’ itself sets off a journey of inner transformation for many.Our exhibition has captured the key moments of his life,” Modani said.The list of activities at the centre is long and diverse. It regularly conducts Sutkatai Prashikshan, which is training in spinning on the charkha—the symbol of self-reliance. It also runs classes in music, painting, sculpture, acting, and other arts. For students who have dropped out of the formal education system, the centre provides special educational support to bring them back into mainstream education. It also offers career guidance and counselling for school and college students.For those interested in deeper study, the centre conducts Grantha Shikshan, which includes study circles on the life and works of Gandhi, Phule, Ambedkar, and saint literature. To propagate the life, work, and philosophy of Gandhiji, it organises lectures, study classes, residential camps, and seminars, while also creating new literature. Its Sujana-Sajag Nagarik Abhiyan is a campaign to create aware, sensitive, and constitutionally committed citizens in the light of Gandhian thought. Besides, the bhavan is also known as the main organiser of the city-level Gandhi jayanti celebrations on Oct 2 at the Mahatma Gandhi statue in Shahganj.Notably, the establishment is entirely self-financed without a single rupee of govt grants, foreign funding, or even public donations—perhaps making it the only such institution in the country.“At a time when Gandhian institutions are struggling, it is our honest attempt to ensure the father of the nation does not remain only in history books, but becomes a living method of personal and social change,” Modani said.He added, “Great scientist Albert Einstein famously said that future generations will scarcely believe that a man like Gandhiji ever walked the earth. As one of our goals, we endeavour to raise our collective understanding of society so that people will actually understand what the words of Einstein mean.”
Article Summary: The Mahatma Gandhi Sarvodaya Bhavan in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar is a hub for Gandhian thought. It is run by 77-year-old Dnyanprakash Modani, who started the centre to coincide with the 150th birth anniversary of Gandhi in 2019. It organises lectures, study classes, residential camps, and seminars, while also creating new literature.

Article Title: Mumbai-bound traffic hit after hatchback catches fire on Vashi Creek bridge
Article Text:
The driver immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine.





NAVI MUMBAI: Vehicular traffic from Navi Mumbai towards Mumbai was disrupted for around 30 minutes after a hatchback caught fire while crossing the Vashi Creek Bridge on Friday at around 7.30pm.The driver escaped unhurt. He immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine. However, the fire soon engulfed the entire vehicle, leaving it completely charred.Vashi traffic police alerted the Vashi fire brigade, which reached the spot within 15 minutes. The charred vehicle was later towed away by a crane, following which traffic movement returned to normal.Sunil Kadam, senior inspector of the Vashi traffic unit, said the driver was identified as Sumit Bhikaji Kadam.“At around 7.45pm, we received a call from one Rahul, whose full name is not known, informing us that a car had caught fire on the Mumbai-bound lane of the Vashi Creek Bridge,” said AV Sisode, the on-duty fireman at Vashi fire station.“In the meantime, we also received a call from the Vashi traffic police and immediately rushed to the spot with a fire tender. The Mumbai fire brigade team had also reached the spot as there was some confusion over the jurisdiction,” Sisode said.The fire was subsequently extinguished, and the Vashi fire brigade team returned to the station at around 8.30pm.
Article Summary: The driver immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine. The fire soon engulfed the entire vehicle, leaving it completely charred. The charred vehicle was later towed away by a crane, following which traffic movement returned to normal.

Article Title: Mumbai-Goa highway crash: 30-year-old killed, 2 cousins injured after Honda City hits gate
Article Text:
30-year-old Akshay Kadam lost his life in a car accident after he lost control of his vehicle





NAVI MUMBAI: A 30-year-old man driving his Honda City car was killed and his two friends, both paternal cousin brothers accompanying him were injured after the driver lost control over the wheels on the Mangaon-Mahad stretch of Mumbai-Goa highway after crossing Mangaon railway station and veering off the road crashed into the iron gate of an industrial unit.The fatal accident occured on Monday around 3 am, when the three friends had gone for dinner at a roadside food stall in Mangaon and were returning to their respective villages in Mahad taluka.The injured complainant stated in the FIR registered at Mangaon police station that the accused car driver and his cousin had consumed liquor before going for dinner.The deceased driver was identified as Akshay Arjun Kadam, a resident of Nandgaon, Mahad taluka. Those injured are Rohit Rajendra Dhadve (24), working as safety officer at Astriel Life Science Pvt Ltd in Mahad MIDC and his cousin Roshan Dilip Dhadve (24). Both residents of Kembhurli, Mahad taluka.Maruti Andhale, senior inspector of Mangaon said, "As the complainant Rohit Dhadve has stated in the FIR that the accused Akshay Kadam drove the car after consuming liquor along with his cousin Roshan, when they had meet near the bus stop, after which they went to Mangaon for dinner, the Motor Vehicle Act section for drunk driving will be invoked.However, as the accused car driver Akshay Kadam responsible for the car crash had died in the accident, a final closure 'Abated summary' report will be submitted before the Mangaon magistrate court. "As per the FIR by the complainant Rohit Dhadve, on Sept 28 around 1 am, when he was at home, his paternal cousin Roshan spoke to him over mobile, when Roshan's maternal cousin Akshay Kadam accompanying him told Rohit that he had come from Mumbai and asked him to meet near the bus stand at Kembhurli.When Rohit met them at the spot, Roshan and Akshay were consuming liquor inside Akshay's Honda City car. Thereafter, Akshay said, "Let's go to Mangaon to have food and the three of them went in the car with Akshay at the wheels."Roshan was sitting beside Akshay and Rohit on the rear seat. They reached Mangaon around 2 am, where they ate parathas at a road side food stall and took parcel of Khima Pav.Thereafter, they drove for 3 kms towards Indapur and took a U-turn to return to their villages in Mahad.After crossing 300 metres from Mangaon railway Station, Akshay lost control over the wheels and yanking off the road on the right side, he crashed into the iron gate of Sundha Steel Traders industrial unit.Rohit sustained injuries below his left eye, left hand and left knee. Akshay got stuck between the driver's seat and the door. Roshan's left leg was injured.Hearing the loud noice of the car crash, the locals gathered, removed the three injured out of the car and summoned 108 ambulance in which they were rushed to Mangaon sub-district hospital, where Akshay was declared brought dead on arrival.
Article Summary: Akshay Arjun Kadam, 30, lost his life in a car accident after he lost control of his vehicle on the Mumbai-Goa highway. His two friends, both paternal cousin brothers accompanying him were injured. The three friends had gone for dinner at a roadside food stall in Mangaon.

Article Title: The mothers adoption forgot: Decades of silence, loss & reunion
Article Text:
Shakti returned home after two months, but never forgot her daughter.

Pune:

What happened to her first daughter?





Shakti remembers walking behind her father on dusty tracks near her village on the outskirts of Pune in the early 1980s—the endless green fields stretching into the distance the day her childhood was taken away.“I didn’t know I was pregnant until I was eight months along,” says the 55-year-old, whose name has been changed to protect her identity. It was her sister-in-law who first noticed the pregnancy. Shakti was 15 when she was raped. “It happened near the sugarcane fields—three times, by the same man, a local farm worker. I didn’t tell anyone. I didn’t know what would come of it.”Her father, devastated and shocked, turned away from her. “Vahini took me to a local doctor, then to a gynaecologist, then to Sassoon Hospital, and finally to a home where I delivered a baby girl.” Around that same time, her father died.“After the birth, they gave me medicine to dry up my milk,” she recalls. “My brother came to take me back. He said the baby would bring shame, that people would ask questions.” Jyoti (name changed) was placed for adoption.Shakti returned home after two months, but never forgot her daughter.Shakti was married off to an older widower, with children almost her age. At 16, she became mother to another daughter.When her husband died, she had to leave home again. Shakti survived through domestic work and odd jobs, raising her child alone.Her secret was buried deep in her bosom. “I never told anyone but my sister-in-law about what happened to me,” she says. “But I always wondered if the child was alive, where she was, what had become of her.”In Germany, Jyoti was being raised by a loving adoptive family. At 15, her curiosity to know her origins led her to begin a search for clues hidden in adoption papers and institutional records. She came across adoption-rights advocates Anjali Pawar and Arun Dohle of the Adoptee Rights Council, who helped trace her birth mother.The trail ended where it had begun decades earlier. Shakti says, “I didn’t want to be found at first.” Memories would resurface, and her “younger daughter still doesn’t know about her half-sister.” But Shakti’s sister-in-law stepped in. Then fear gave way to hope. In 2016, Jyoti arrived in India and the reunion took place with discretion.Jyoti clearly remembers the day. “My mother was in a flower-printed sari and had a large red bindi.” Beside her stood Shakti’s vahini, her confidante of many years. Seated across Shakti was the daughter she had thought of every day of her life for 30 years. Mother and daughter broke down in tears.Shakti gently caressed her daughter’s head and wiped off her tears with her pallu as the two embraced. “It was the first time in my life someone truly knew. I didn’t have to hide anymore...,” she says.Yet not every story ends this way. For instance, Baani (name changed) — her daughter was given up for adoption after her family refused to accept an inter-caste relationship. Decades later, the daughter traced her to Nagpur. Baani blessed her daughter but asked that they never meet again. She feared the taboo of being an unwed mother. She died in Oct 2023.Then there was Dhanalakshmi of Chennai who spent decades grieving her two lost sons to unconsented adoption. She died last month, not long after reuniting with one of her sons.
Article Summary: Shakti was 15 when she was raped by the same man, a local farm worker. She was married off to an older widower, with children almost her age. At 16, she became mother to another daughter. Shakti survived through domestic work and odd jobs, raising her child alone.

Article Title: Delhi-based gang attempts to break open flats in Baner society; one nabbed
Article Text:
An AI-generated illustration of a gang of thieves attempting to break into multiple apartments

Pune:





Baner police have arrested Ramkishor Dabla (26), a resident of Bakkarwala in Delhi, after a gang attempted to break open several flats in a housing society in Baner around 2.30 am on Saturday.Police have also launched a search for his three accomplices. Chandrashekar Sawant, senior inspector of Baner police station, said, “The residents of the society woke up after the noises due to the break-in attempts by the suspects. They then alerted police.”The patrolling team reached the society and nabbed Dabla, while three others fled in the dark. Sawant said, “No item was stolen, but the suspects broke open locks of several flats.”“The flat owners have gone out of station, and they informed us that nothing costly was kept in their flats. We suspect that the gang is operating in Delhi and they decided to try their luck in Pune. We have been questioning Dabla about this,” he said.“We are checking if the Delhi police have their detail and crime records,” he said.
Article Summary: Baner police have arrested Ramkishor Dabla (26), a resident of Bakkarwala in Delhi. Police have also launched a search for his three accomplices. No item was stolen, but the suspects broke open locks of several flats.

Article Title: Motorcycle rider gives lift to minor, got bullet in the back
Article Text:
Representative image

Pune:





A 28-year-old civil services aspirant from Ambegaon Budruk, off Katraj-Dehu Road bypass, sustained a bullet wound to his lower back after a 16-year-old boy, to whom he had offered a lift on his motorcycle, accidentally opened fire while handling his country-made pistol around 2 pm on Friday.After recording a statement from the civil services aspirant, Bibvewadi police filed a suo motu complaint against the boy on Saturday evening. Police served a notice to the boy and seized the country-made pistol also.Senior inspector Ashwini Satpute of Bibvewadi police station said, “The civil services aspirant and the boy, a resident of Kasewadi, know each other as they keep meeting regularly. On Friday afternoon, the boy sought a lift from him in the Bibvewadi area and requested him to drop him near Shankarseth Road. The civil services aspirant, who was heading towards his classes in the Peth area of the city, stopped his motorcycle and the minor boy sat pillion. ”“While travelling towards the old part of the city, the motorcycle reached Gangadham Chowk when the minor boy, who was continuously making movements while sitting pillion because of the pistol in his trousers, decided to pull out the pistol. However, while doing so, he accidentally pulled the trigger,” she said.“The bullet hit the lower back of the civil services aspirant while he was riding the motorcycle. The motorcycle rider lost his balance, and both fell on the road. Passersby raised an alarm, and our team reached the spot. They took the minor to the police station and the injured motorcycle rider to the hospital. He is out of danger,” she said.The boy, according to the police, is a school dropout and does not work. His parents are daily-wage workers. “We will question him from where he got the pistol and what the purpose was behind having the pistol,” Satpute said.The rising involvement of juveniles in firearm-related crimes has emerged as a serious concern for Pune Police, with multiple incidents in 2026 highlighting the ease with which minors are gaining access to illegal weapons. In Feb, a 17-year-old out on bail in a murder case and three minor accomplices were detained in the Katraj-Dias Plot area after allegedly firing two rounds in the air to terrorise residents. In July, the Pune Crime Branch detained a minor along with older gang operatives linked to extortion threats issued in the name of the Lawrence Bishnoi gang, recovering foreign-made Turkish and Chinese pistols. Police investigations indicated that young offenders were increasingly being used by organised criminal networks for intimidation and violent activities.The trend continued in Sept with two separate incidents involving teenagers. In Swargate, police caught two 17-year-olds with previous attempted murder cases near the Mutha Right Bank Canal carrying a country-made pistol and live ammunition. Days later in Kondhwa, a 16-year-old allegedly mistook a 28-year-old interior designer for a rival and shot him before fleeing with another minor accomplice. According to Pune Police, several of the illicit country-made firearms surfacing in such cases are being smuggled into the city from manufacturing hubs in Madhya Pradesh, underscoring growing concerns over illegal gun trafficking and juvenile access to weapons.
Article Summary: A 28-year-old civil services aspirant from Ambegaon Budruk sustained a bullet wound to his lower back. The boy, 16, accidentally opened fire while handling his country-made pistol. The rising involvement of juveniles in firearm-related crimes has emerged as a serious concern for Pune Police.
